grade.first_issue: The first score-controlling defect is the necessity argument in Step 4. The assertion that Mulan can only create angles of the form φ+mθ+k·180° is neither defined nor proved and is not justified when each cut parameter is an arbitrary real number. Merely choosing initial angles outside a countable set does not show that Shan-Yu can preserve avoidance of θ after every possible cut. This omits the central adversarial invariant/response argument, so Rule E caps the score at 3.
grade.summary: The final classification θ=180°/n for integers n≥2 is correct. The peeling construction for an angle nθ is also correct, and the sufficiency strategy has the right main idea. However, Move B is not admissible merely from γ<θ: with α1=180°−β−θ=α+γ−θ one also needs α+γ>θ (for example, θ=60° and (α,β,γ)=(10°,150°,20°) gives α1<0). This can be repaired locally by choosing the larger of the other two angles as the apex. The decisive problem is necessity: no valid invariant or strategy for Shan-Yu is established, and the countability statement cannot replace the required proof that every cut has a safe child. Supplying that marked-angle lemma and its four-case verification is a new central argument, not a routine omission.
strengths: States the correct complete set of values.
Correctly computes the angle triples resulting from a cut.
Correctly observes that an angle nθ can be peeled to (n−1)θ while the other child contains θ.
Contains the main framework of a valid sufficiency strategy.

errors.description: Move B is falsely claimed to be legal whenever γ<θ; positivity of α1 additionally requires α+γ>θ. This is a load-bearing but locally repairable Rule C error.

The necessity direction rests on an undefined and unsupported affine/countability claim. It does not prove that Shan-Yu has a legal safe response to every cut, so the exclusion of all θ not dividing 180° is unproved. Rule E applies.

The statement for θ<60° that repeated Move A can first produce an angle below θ is not actually demonstrated or qualified for the case where repeated subtraction reaches θ exactly, although this portion could be repaired by a short induction.
